name: Erik Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Erik, thanks for talking with me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. Shall we start?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, fine by me. I've got the afternoon.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate Norwegian and Danish into English, almost all of it to do with ships. Inspection reports for ship classification, which is the check that says a vessel is fit to sail, crew contracts, and safety procedures for offshore supply boats. Most of it comes from a maritime translation agency, and a shipping insurer sends me claims documents directly. I work in my flat near the harbour, and I can see the ferries from my desk, which helps when I'm stuck on a word.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like it when I understand a ship better because of a report. My father was a ship's engineer for thirty years, so I grew up with engine rooms, and sometimes I phone him to ask what a part actually does. What's hard is that I'm slow and still learning. The agency's reviewer, a woman called Sigrid, sends back maybe a third of my files with corrections, and she's usually right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. Steady as she goes, then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the tools help with the dull bits and the rest still needs people who know ships. I'd say it at choir practice over coffee if anyone asked. I'm not one for posting opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. The agency already gives me machine drafts for the repetitive certificates, and they save me an hour a day, nothing more. My flat's nearly paid off, and I've got about a year of savings. Plenty of maritime agencies in this city if one dries up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep using the agency's machine drafts where they're reliable. I'd ask Sigrid for a monthly half-hour to go over my mistakes, so I improve faster. And I'd keep paying extra off the flat, about 300 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, mostly. It's a decent life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you come to have a nearly paid-off flat at twenty-seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father helped with the deposit when I finished university, and I've paid it down hard since. My father says a man should own his roof before he owns anything else. I think he's right, though I'd never say it to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anyone you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not many. Maybe Sigrid, the reviewer, because checking is what these tools are trying to do. But in this picture even she keeps her job.

I'd say it at **choir practice** over coffee, not online.

Plenty of **maritime agencies** in this city if one dries up.
do: Keep using the agency's **machine drafts** on repetitive certificates.
Ask the reviewer for a **monthly half-hour** on his mistakes.
Pay about **300 a month** extra off the flat.
feel: **Calm** and mostly content with a decent life.

fieldNote: His **father's values** run through his money choices.
He uses AI **now and then**, only where it's proven reliable.
Wants to **learn faster** from his reviewer, Sigrid.

steps.text: Keep using the agency's machine drafts on repetitive certificates
Ask the agency reviewer for a monthly mistakes session
Pay about 300 a month extra off the flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That's more like weather coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's how markets work: new tools come in, and people who work hard adjust. I'd say the government shouldn't try to stop it, but schools and firms should offer proper apprenticeships for people who need to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my documents are about as standard as documents get: the same forms, the same phrases, the same ships. A machine plus Sigrid could do the agency's whole volume. I'm junior and slow, so I think I'd lose half my agency work in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the machine drafts on everything, not just the certificates, so at least I'm as fast as the others. I'd save harder, about 500 a month, and stop the extra payments on the flat so I have cash. And I'd ask the insurer if they'd take me on staff, checking claims, because they seem slower to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not in a dramatic way. I'd be sleeping all right but thinking about it on my walks along the harbour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your father say about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say, 'Then learn something they can't do with a computer.' He's said versions of that since I chose languages. My father fixed ship engines for thirty years and never once worried a computer would take his job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government shouldn't stop it. What if it's your job going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still, no. I don't think it's the state's job to protect my translations. I'd rather they paid for apprenticeships, so I can earn my way into something else.

steps.text: Use the agency's machine drafts on every file

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's a gale, not weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to roll up their sleeves, and firms should hire apprentices instead of waiting for robots. I'd still say I don't want handouts. But I'd want help with training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my work is pure thinking work, so it ends by 2028, staff job or not. What lasts is the hands-on side of ships, for about three years more until robots come in around 2031. So the harbour outside my window is where the work is, not the desk in front of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply straight away to the shipyard's marine electrician apprenticeship, where my father knows people. I'd live on savings and the low apprentice wage for the first year, which is why I'd stop all extra spending now. And I'd ask my father to teach me what he can on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake for a while. But having the shipyard nearby gives me somewhere to point myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your father feel about you asking for his help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pleased, I think, and a bit smug. He's been waiting nine years for me to come down to the engine room. My father would say 'about time', and then he'd teach me properly, because that's what he's like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three years until robots. Isn't an apprenticeship a short road?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might be. But robots still need fixing, and ships are messy, wet places. I'd rather be a young electrician when the robots arrive than an out-of-work translator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. More like a long swell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, but with more patience: five years is enough for anyone willing to work. I'd tell the young people at the sailing club to think about trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd get three or four more years of translating, getting better and saving. Then by 2031 I'd want to be through most of an apprenticeship. Robots on ships don't come until about 2034, so the timing could work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating full-time for now and use the machine drafts more. I'd start the marine electrician course in the evenings next autumn, which is two years part-time. And I'd keep saving 400 a month for the year when I'm on apprentice pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a working sort of way. Like a job list on the fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gives, to fit an evening course in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Choir, probably, at least for a year. That's the one I'd mind. The sailing club I'd keep, because I'd go mad without the water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get better at translating. Why bother, if it ends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't like doing a job badly, even a job that's ending. Sigrid would still be sending files back otherwise. And better work pays more, and that money pays for the switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Calm seas, more or less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time for people to plan, and nobody should wait for the government to plan it for them. I'd say it at choir and at the club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thirty-seven when it arrives. That's young enough for a trade, and I'd have most of a decade to save first. The next few years would look like now, just with better tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating and use the AI tools more as they prove themselves. I'd finish paying off the flat, maybe by 2030. And around 2031 I'd start the electrician course, so I'm qualified before the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. It's there at the back. Mostly I'd get on with things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about a family in that timeline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to, yes. I'd want to be settled in a trade before I have children, so they're not growing up while I'm starting over. That's maybe the biggest thing the extra years give me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sigrid, the reviewer, honestly. She's fifty and she's good at exactly the thing the machines get good at. I don't know what she'd do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be starting an apprenticeship at twenty-nine on a wage I couldn't live on without savings. What would help is apprenticeships for adults that pay a real wage, and firms willing to take on someone who's late to the trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who's responsible when a translated safety procedure is wrong. A man on a supply boat in a storm reads the safety page I translated. Somebody with a name should stand behind every word on it.

headlineQuote: A man on a supply boat in a storm reads the safety page I translated. Somebody with a name should stand behind every word on it.
portrait: Erik is a 27-year-old **Norwegian and Danish** translator of ship inspection reports and crew documents.
His father, a ship's engineer, helped him buy a **nearly paid-off flat** by the harbour.
He uses **AI tools** once proven and believes in work and apprenticeships, not handouts.
In faster scenarios he'd train as a **marine electrician**, using the robot delay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, starting an apprenticeship at twenty-nine on a thin wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Adult apprenticeships** that pay a real wage.
Firms willing to hire someone **late to the trade**.
